### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to mitigate contextual drag without training. Contextual drag refers to the phenomenon where prior context disproportionately influences subsequent reasoning or generation. Paper [13] ("Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study") explicitly studies anchoring bias, which is a cognitive bias where initial information disproportionately influences decisions. While [13] focuses on identifying and experimentally studying anchoring bias, it does not propose a method to mitigate it. No other prior paper explicitly addresses the purpose of mitigating contextual drag without training. Therefore, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Draft De-anchoring Decoding (D3), uses dual key-value caches (draft-present and draft-redacted prompts) and interpolates their logits at each decoding step to attenuate harmful anchoring. Paper [5] ("The Hidden Cost of Structured Generation in LLMs: Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding") introduces Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding (DCCD), which uses draft-conditioned decoding to enforce validity during structured generation. While DCCD employs draft-conditioned mechanisms, it does not use dual key-value caches or interpolation of logits to address anchoring bias. Paper [6] ("Draft Model Knows When to Stop: Self-Verification Speculative Decoding for Long-Form Generation") and [7] ("Speculative Decoding with CTC-based Draft Model for LLM Inference Acceleration") also use draft models in speculative decoding frameworks, but their mechanisms focus on inference acceleration and draft verification rather than mitigating anchoring bias. No prior paper uses the same mechanism of dual key-value caches and logit interpolation for de-anchoring. Therefore, the mechanism is **not covered**.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its method on the Game of 24 with Qwen3-8B against pre-registered success criteria. Papers [6], [7], [10], [11], and [17] all use speculative decoding frameworks and evaluate their methods on reasoning tasks, often with pre-registered success criteria or benchmarks. For example, [6] evaluates speculative decoding methods for long-form generation, and [11] evaluates adaptive draft length in speculative decoding. While the specific benchmark (Game of 24) and model (Qwen3-8B) are new, the evaluation design — using reasoning tasks with pre-registered success criteria — is covered by these prior papers. Therefore, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of decoding-time intervention for LLM reasoning. Paper [2] ("CARE: Decoding Time Safety Alignment via Rollback and Introspection Intervention") explicitly addresses decoding-time interventions for LLM safety, and papers [6], [7], [10], [11], and [17] all focus on decoding-time interventions for LLM inference acceleration or reasoning. While the specific sub-problem (contextual drag mitigation) is new, the general domain of decoding-time intervention for LLM reasoning is well-covered by prior work. Therefore, the domain is **covered**.
